title: How does a harmful deed return to the doer?
claim: Across the chapters on fearing evil deeds, not harming, not coveting, not stealing and clean action, the return of harm is described in several distinct ways rather than one. Its inescapability is spatial in 207 and 208 (the enmity of deeds follows and kills, ruin stays at the foot like a shadow, both with வீயாது), and 313 sharpens it with உய்யா: an enemy can be survived, one's own hurtful act cannot. It is temporal in 319 (forenoon harm comes back in the afternoon, தாமே, of itself), an agent's act in 204 (அறம் plots the plotter's ruin), and a near-tautology of desire in 206 and 320 (whoever wants no pain causes none). A separate figure, the ripening, places the harm at the harvest and not at the getting: coveted gain in 177, theft in 284, and forbidden deeds that succeed in 658 all go bad at விளைவு, and 659 extends the return to wealth taken with tears, while adding that rightly got wealth pays later even if lost.
limits: The thread describes how the return is pictured, not whether the book thinks it always happens; 169 concedes that the crooked prosper and the upright fall, which thread:justice_of_the_world takes up. Who or what returns the harm (அறம் in 204, nobody in 319, Parimelazhagar's அறக்கடவுள் and pāvam in his glosses) is left unsettled by the verses.

title: One checklist for action, from the king's deed to the minister's definition
claim: A short list of conditions for successful action recurs across five Porul chapters and changes role as it moves. In 483 means and time (கருவி, காலம்) make any 'hard deed' (அருவினை) possible; 631 reuses the same three words but turns them into the definition of a minister, adding method (செய்கை); 675 expands them into a five-item rule for anyone acting (resources, means, time, deed, place); and 516, in the chapter on employing people, keeps deed and time and adds the one item the others lack, the doer. A parallel pair, 461 and 676, shares the closing command (சூழ்ந்து / பார்த்துச் செயல்) and the yield as its last term, but 461 counts loss against gain while 676 weighs the course of the work, its completion and obstacles. Read together, the minister's defining skill is the general checklist for action, and the book adjusts the list to the chapter it sits in.
limits: This is a claim about recurring vocabulary and list structure, not that the lists are meant as one doctrine; Parimelazhagar glosses the items differently in each place (in 675 each term covers both one's own side and the enemy's). It does not cover the separate theme of execution failing after sound planning (640, 664).

title: Can a single virtue stand without the rest?
claim: Several verses isolate one restraint and say it keeps its value even when the rest of virtue is absent, using a shared 'even if he does wrong' frame: not desiring another's wife in 150 (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும்) and not backbiting in 181 (அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும்), with 142 ranking the adulterer lowest among those outside virtue. 297 goes further for not lying, saying the other virtues may be left undone, and 296 gives the reason: not lying yields all the virtues by itself. Yet 321 answers 'what is virtuous action?' with not killing, and 33 tells one to do virtue everywhere and without break. Because the book makes this move for different virtues, the verses read best as emphasis on each chapter's virtue, and Parimelazhagar on 150 and 181 says only that the one quality 'stands out' despite the faults, not that it suffices.
limits: Only 296-297 claim sufficiency; 150 and 181 claim only that the one abstention is still good. Parimelazhagar reconciles 297 with 33 by reading it as advice to keep one virtue unfailingly rather than fail at many, and 323 itself ranks not killing above not lying (see thread:competing_supremes and thread:truth_by_effect).

title: Does virtue yield wealth, or wealth yield virtue?
claim: Book 1 says virtue yields distinction and wealth (31, சிறப்பு ஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்), and Book 2 turns the same construction round: wealth that came by knowing the means and without wrong yields virtue and pleasure (754, அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்), and for those who amass bright wealth the other two come easily together (760). The reversal holds only with a condition on how the wealth was got: 754's தீதின்றி fits wealth into 39's rule that only pleasure through virtue is pleasure, 659 says what is taken with tears leaves with tears, and 1009 uses 760's own word ஒண்பொருள் for wealth amassed by ignoring virtue, which others carry off. So the two books do not rank the ends differently; they make the causal arrow run both ways and let the manner of acquisition decide which way it runs.
limits: The condition is explicit in 754 but only read into 760 by Parimelazhagar, who glosses ஒண்பொருள் there as wealth that comes by the right way; on its face 760 promises virtue to abundance as such. Parimelazhagar also reads 754 as a king's revenue raised without tyranny, so its scope may be royal wealth only.
